title: Can someone help explain Synecdoche New York?

commenti.body:
>I’ve read other interpretations but nothing rly answers everything. I can get that this may not be the point of the film to some people, but everything is clearly there for a reason imo. Can anyone help explain?

Are you looking for an explanation of the film's plot (IE the series of events in its fictional world) or for something more like an interpretation of it as an artwork (IE what kind of meaning we might take away from it)? Those are two separate but related questions.

I'd say, off the bat, that a big part of this film and its possible meaning comes from its ambiguity. This is a film very much about its own artifice, about the fuzzy boundaries between reality and fiction. One interpretation is that this is a film about filmmaking or, more broadly, about the creative process. The gigantic warehouse housing the protagonist's elaborate reconstruction of his New York is a physical literalization of what all artists are trying to do -- reproduce the world and human life, in all its complexity, in miniature. I think of James Joyce's famous description of one of his main artistic goals when writing *Ulysses*:

>a picture of Dublin so complete that if the city one day suddenly disappeared from the earth it could be reconstructed out of my book.
I kinda thought of it like “to make an apple pie from scratch one must first create the universe”. His ideas kept getting bigger and bigger and he got lost in them and his own neuroses

I love this movie, but for me it is something to be experienced, not explained. 

You say you have no idea how to feel - but how and what did the movie make you feel? 

I think it's an absurdist piece of art meant to question what is real and what is imagined in our own lives. 

I like this video essay on the movie: 

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j1LZ9EOMqsY
](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j1LZ9EOMqsY)

>what all artists are trying to do -- reproduce the world and human life, in all its complexity, in miniature

May I respectfully disagree. Barnett Newman put it this way: what an artist does is to CREATE reality.

Edited to address that.

However, you must admit that mimesis has been an artistic goal in many different time periods, cultures and media. And that mimesis itself is arguably a central theme if not the central theme of *Synecdoche, New York*.

YMS on YouTube did a brilliant 5 part series called "The Genius of Synecdoche NY where he breaks down the minutiae of the movie scene by scene. It is very long and super in depth but if you're interested in Synecdoche and the symbolism and themes it is a wonderful wild ride.

My initial read of it was about how anxiety, depression and self-doubt sabotage your life. Sometimes these insidious neurotic features of a person can really ruin good things. 

The phenomenon seems pretty common IRL but is not too explored in movies—at least in the over the top Kaufman way—. We see this when people are so worried their romantic relationship might fail that they themselves fuck it up and cause it to do just that.

To me, it’s a film about how neurosis literally sabotages all aspects of your life. A much better Beau is Afraid

>mimesis itself is arguably a central theme

Dedekind, the mathematician, came up with the idea that the perfect map of London would have to include itself. The idea is the play within the play going on forever that is an expression of what we fancifully might call the "metaphysical immanence," the realness of everything that could possibly exist.  I am basing this idea on Spinoza and Leibniz, formative influences in this whole style of thought.

That reminds me of this famous Borgesian passage, which I think has obvious affinities to the film:

>…In that Empire, the Art of Cartography attained such Perfection that the map of a single Province occupied the entirety of a City, and the map of the Empire, the entirety of a Province. In time, those Unconscionable Maps no longer satisfied, and the Cartographers Guilds struck a Map of the Empire whose size was that of the Empire, and which coincided point for point with it. The following Generations, who were not so fond of the Study of Cartography as their Forebears had been, saw that that vast Map was Useless, and not without some Pitilessness was it, that they delivered it up to the Inclemencies of Sun and Winters. In the Deserts of the West, still today, there are Tattered Ruins of that Map, inhabited by Animals and Beggars; in all the Land there is no other Relic of the Disciplines of Geography.
Exactly true -- Borges was inspired by the stuff I mentioned.  And obviously Synecdoche is reading Borges.
Yeah I thinking exactly this. YMS loves this movie. I’m sure he went into this in detail
I’d say there’s a difference between anxiety/depression and actually not knowing that years have gone by.
It made me feel like wanting to know what happened in the movie. I understand your perspective as I said, but if art is laid out like this it’s also asking for specific interpretation.
